docs.title: CBOR PHP
docs.text:
CBOR, the Concise Binary Object Representation of RFC 8949, is a binary data format built on a data model close to the one JSON describes, with a few things JSON lacks: byte strings, a tag mechanism that carries meaning, and an encoding small enough for a constrained device.

CBOR PHP encodes and decodes it. Every major type of the specification is implemented, definite and indefinite length alike, with the tags of the IANA registry that applications actually meet and a way to write the ones they do not.

use CBOR\Decoder;
use CBOR\MapObject;
use CBOR\StringStream;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;

$map = MapObject::create()
    ->add(TextStringObject::create('name'), TextStringObject::create('John Doe'))
    ->add(TextStringObject::create('age'), UnsignedIntegerObject::create(30));

$encoded = (string) $map;

$decoded = Decoder::create()->decode(StringStream::create($encoded));

$data = $decoded->normalize();
// ['name' => 'John Doe', 'age' => '30']

docs.title: What CBOR buys you
docs.text:
• It is compact. Smaller than JSON for most data, and no base64 detour for bytes.
  • It is quick. A binary encoding, read and written without a text parser.
  • It carries meaning. A tag says what a value is: an instant, a big integer, a URI, a signed message.
  • It is specified. One specification, one registry of tags held by IANA.
  • It holds everything. Every major type, binary data included.

docs.title: Where you meet it
docs.text:
• WebAuthn and FIDO2: the attestation objects and the authenticator data of a credential.
  • COSE: signing and encryption, the CBOR counterpart of JOSE.
  • CWT: CBOR Web Tokens, where JWT would use JSON.
  • CoAP: the payloads of the protocol constrained devices speak.
  • The Internet of things: sensor readings, on a link that counts its bytes.
  • APIs: a binary answer where JSON costs too much.

docs.title: The Symfony bundle
docs.text:
spomky-labs/cbor-bundle wires this library into a Symfony application. Version 3.1 of the bundle is the one that pairs with version 3.3 of the library: it exposes the decoder as a service, and lets the container register tag classes of your own.

composer require spomky-labs/cbor-bundle

Symfony Flex registers it. Without Flex, add it to config/bundles.php:

return [
    // …
    SpomkyLabs\CborBundle\SpomkyLabsCborBundle::class => ['all' => true],
];

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
SpomkyLabs\CborBundle\CBORDecoder takes the bytes and returns the object tree, so the stream is handled for you:

use SpomkyLabs\CborBundle\CBORDecoder;

final class PayloadController
{
    public function __construct(
        private readonly CBORDecoder $decoder,
    ) {
    }

    public function __invoke(Request $request): Response
    {
        $document = $this->decoder->decode($request->getContent());

        return $this->json($document->normalize());
    }
}

CBOR\Decoder itself is a service too, for the calls the wrapper does not cover.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
One option, the nesting depth the decoder accepts:

# config/packages/cbor.yaml
cbor:
    max_depth: 1000 # the default

Lower it when the payloads come from somewhere you do not control:

cbor:
    max_depth: 32

docs.title: Tags of your own
docs.text:
A class implementing CBOR\Tag\TagInterface — see writing a tag of your own — joins the decoder's tag manager when its service carries the cbor.tag tag. Major type 7 items work the same way, with CBOR\OtherObjectInterface and cbor.other_object:

services:
    App\Cbor\CustomTag:
        tags: ['cbor.tag']

    App\Cbor\CustomObject:
        tags: ['cbor.other_object']

The container only reads the class of such a service definition; the decoder instantiates it itself, with the data of the item it is reading.

The next version does much more

Version 3.2 of the bundle integrates CBOR into the Symfony Serializer — $serializer->serialize($data, 'cbor'), objects, enums, and the encoding options as context keys. It requires version 3.4 of the library, so it is documented in the 3.4 version of this site.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
A few rules make a review quick:

  • You MUST follow the PSR-12 coding standards.
  • You MUST run the test suite.
  • You MUST write, or update, unit tests when a bug is fixed or a feature is added.
  • You SHOULD write documentation.

Open a pull request against the branch of the version concerned — a fix on the oldest branch that has the bug, a feature on the newest — write commit messages that make sense, and rebase before submitting. You may be asked to squash.

The checks that gate a pull request all run locally through Castor, in the same image the CI uses:

composer install
castor ecs        # coding standards (castor ecs_fix to apply)
castor rector     # automated refactoring, dry run (castor rector_fix to apply)
castor phpstan    # static analysis
castor deptrac    # architecture layers
castor lint       # syntax check
castor phpunit    # tests, with coverage

The full version is in CONTRIBUTING.md, and what is expected of everyone taking part is in the code of conduct.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
The first question about a CBOR document is usually what is in it. A decoded tree answers that directly:

// The whole shape
var_dump($object);

// Entry by entry, for a map or a list
foreach ($map as $item) {
    echo sprintf(
        "Key: %s, Value: %s\n",
        $item->getKey()->normalize(),
        $item->getValue()->normalize()
    );
}

// What it encodes to
$encoded = (string) $object;
echo 'Hex: ' . bin2hex($encoded) . "\n";
echo 'Length: ' . strlen($encoded) . " bytes\n";

Printing the class of each object is often faster than printing its value: get_class($object) tells you whether that number came in as a tagged instant or a plain integer, and whether a string arrived in definite or indefinite-length form.

docs.title: Reading the bytes
docs.text: A CBOR head is one byte: the three high bits are the major type, the five low bits the additional information. bin2hex() and the table of major types are enough to read the start of a document by hand — a2 is a map of two entries, d9 d9 f7 the self-described CBOR tag.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• Build one decoder and keep it. Decoder::create() assembles the tag and simple-value managers every time it is called. A decoder holds no state about the document it reads, so one instance serves a whole request, or a whole process.
  • Pick the narrowest type. The head of an item is as short as the value allows: a small integer in an UnsignedIntegerObject costs one byte, the same number written as a 64-bit value costs nine.
  • Build a collection once. Add the items as you go, rather than rebuilding a list or a map to change one entry.
  • Stream what is large. Indefinite-length objects let a producer start writing before it knows the total length, and a reader take it in as it arrives.
  • Install ext-gmp. It is what brick/math uses as its fastest calculator; without it the big number tags convert their byte strings in quadratic time. ext-bcmath is needed by the decimal fraction and bigfloat tags in any case.

docs.title: What the decoder costs
docs.text:
Decoding is proportional to the bytes it reads, with two exceptions, both of them tags: the big number tags, whose conversion to a decimal string is a base conversion, and the fractional number tags, whose value expands with their exponent. Both are bounded for that reason — see the cost of a hostile document — and both bounds can be made tighter than the defaults by your own validation if your protocol allows it.

Encoding costs one pass over the tree. The head of a list or a map carries the number of items it holds, which every insertion invalidates: the library recomputes it when the object is written out, not on each call, so building a large container stays linear.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
// Encoding
$text = TextStringObject::create('hello');
$int = UnsignedIntegerObject::create(42);
$list = ListObject::create([$text, $int]);
$map = MapObject::create()->add($text, $int);
$tagged = TimestampTag::create($int);
$encoded = (string) $map;

// Decoding
$decoder = Decoder::create();
$stream = StringStream::create($encoded);
$object = $decoder->decode($stream);
$phpValue = $object->normalize();

// Tags
$timestamp = TimestampTag::create(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(time()));
$decimal = DecimalFractionTag::createFromFloat(3.14);
$datetime = DatetimeTag::create(TextStringObject::create('2024-01-15T10:30:00Z'));

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
• RFC 8949 — Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), the current specification. It replaced RFC 7049, which the library's older keywords still mention.
  • IANA CBOR tags registry — which number means what, and who registered it.
  • RFC 8610 — CDDL, a notation for writing down the shape a CBOR document must have.

docs.title: What is built on it
docs.text:
• RFC 9052 — COSE, signing and encryption in CBOR. It replaced RFC 8152.
  • RFC 8392 — CWT, CBOR Web Tokens.
  • RFC 7252 — CoAP, whose payloads are often CBOR.
  • RFC 8428 — SenML, sensor measurements.
  • WebAuthn — attestation objects and COSE keys.

docs.title: Normalization
docs.text:
A decoded document is a tree of objects, which says exactly how the data was encoded. An application usually wants the values instead. Objects that can give them implement the Normalizable interface, whose normalize() method returns a native PHP value:

$text = TextStringObject::create('Hello');
$text->normalize(); // string: "Hello"

$int = UnsignedIntegerObject::create(42);
$int->normalize(); // string: "42"

$map = MapObject::create()
    ->add(TextStringObject::create('key'), UnsignedIntegerObject::create(100));
$map->normalize(); // array: ['key' => '100']

Normalizing a list or a map normalizes what it holds, so one call on the decoded root gives the whole document as PHP arrays and scalars.

An integer normalizes to a string

CBOR integers run to 64 bits unsigned, and the bignum tags further still, which is wider than the integers of PHP on every platform. normalize() therefore returns a numeric string for every integer, small ones included: a value never silently loses its precision on the way out. Cast it yourself when you know it fits, or hand the string to brick/math.

A few objects have nothing to normalize to, and say so by not implementing the interface: the tags that only announce how a byte string is meant to be written out, for instance (tags 21, 22 and 23), hand back the object they wrap through getValue() instead.

Normalization is also where a hostile document can cost the most, because a few tags expand far beyond the bytes they occupy. The bounds that keep that in check are described in the cost of a hostile document.

docs.title: The data model
docs.text:
A CBOR data item is one of eight major types, numbered 0 to 7. Every one of them has a class in this library, and some have two: one for the definite-length encoding, one for the indefinite-length form.

Type Description PHP classes 0 Unsigned integer UnsignedIntegerObject 1 Negative integer NegativeIntegerObject 2 Byte string ByteStringObject, IndefiniteLengthByteStringObject 3 Text string TextStringObject, IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject 4 Array ListObject, IndefiniteLengthListObject 5 Map MapObject, IndefiniteLengthMapObject 6 Tag subclasses of Tag, see tags 7 Simple value or float TrueObject, FalseObject, NullObject, the float objects

Every class lives in the CBOR namespace, the tags in CBOR\Tag, and the simple values and floats in CBOR\OtherObject.

docs.title: The hierarchy of classes
docs.text:
CBORObject (interface)
└── AbstractCBORObject (abstract)
    ├── UnsignedIntegerObject
    ├── NegativeIntegerObject
    ├── ByteStringObject
    ├── IndefiniteLengthByteStringObject
    ├── TextStringObject
    ├── IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject
    ├── ListObject
    ├── IndefiniteLengthListObject
    ├── MapObject
    ├── IndefiniteLengthMapObject
    ├── Tag (abstract)
    │   ├── DatetimeTag
    │   ├── TimestampTag
    │   ├── DecimalFractionTag
    │   ├── BigFloatTag
    │   ├── … the other built-in tags
    │   └── GenericTag
    └── OtherObject (abstract)
        ├── TrueObject
        ├── FalseObject
        ├── NullObject
        ├── UndefinedObject
        ├── DoublePrecisionFloatObject
        └── …

Two things are true of every object of that tree, whatever its type:

  • it is built by a static create() method, never by new;
  • casting it to a string encodes it, because each one implements __toString().

Most of them also implement Normalizable, which turns a decoded object into a native PHP value. That is the subject of normalization.

docs.title: API responses
docs.text:
CBOR has a media type of its own, application/cbor, and an answer in it is built the same way as any other document: a map, encoded, written out.

use CBOR\MapObject;
use CBOR\NegativeIntegerObject;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;
use InvalidArgumentException;

function encodeToCBOR(array $data): string
{
    $map = MapObject::create();

    foreach ($data as $key => $value) {
        $keyObject = TextStringObject::create((string) $key);
        $valueObject = match (gettype($value)) {
            'string' => TextStringObject::create($value),
            'integer' => $value >= 0
                ? UnsignedIntegerObject::create($value)
                : NegativeIntegerObject::create($value),
            'array' => convertArrayToList($value),
            default => throw new InvalidArgumentException(sprintf('Unsupported type "%s"', gettype($value))),
        };

        $map->add($keyObject, $valueObject);
    }

    return (string) $map;
}

$response = encodeToCBOR([
    'status' => 'success',
    'code' => 200,
    'data' => ['item1', 'item2'],
]);

header('Content-Type: application/cbor');
echo $response;

A converter like this one is a decision about your protocol, not a feature of the format: what types you accept, what you do with a float, whether a date becomes a tagged instant or a string. Write the mapping down and keep both ends to it — which is the whole difference between a binary protocol and a guess.

The way back, for a request body:

use CBOR\Decoder;
use CBOR\StringStream;

// 32 levels of nesting is plenty for a request body
$decoder = Decoder::create(null, null, 32);

try {
    $document = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create($requestBody));
} catch (InvalidArgumentException) {
    http_response_code(400);
    exit;
}

$data = $document->normalize();

The depth limit and the try block are not optional on a public endpoint: see the cost of a hostile document.

docs.title: COSE
docs.text:
COSE, RFC 9052, is what JOSE is for JSON: signed, MACed and encrypted messages, written in CBOR. A COSE_Sign1 — one signer, the common case — is an array of four items, usually wrapped in tag 18.

use CBOR\Decoder;
use CBOR\ListObject;
use CBOR\StringStream;
use CBOR\Tag;

$decoded = Decoder::create()->decode(StringStream::create($binaryData));

// Tag 18 is not registered in this version: a tagged message arrives as a GenericTag.
$message = $decoded instanceof Tag ? $decoded->getValue() : $decoded;

if (! $message instanceof ListObject || count($message) !== 4) {
    throw new RuntimeException('A COSE_Sign1 is an array of four items');
}

$protected = $message->get(0)->getValue();   // bytes: a CBOR map, encoded
$unprotected = $message->get(1);             // a map, in the clear
$payload = $message->get(2)->getValue();     // bytes, or null
$signature = $message->get(3)->getValue();   // bytes

The protected header is a byte string that holds an encoded CBOR map, and the payload is a byte string too. That is deliberate: the signature covers those exact bytes. Decode the protected header to read it, never to rewrite it.

$headers = Decoder::create()->decode(StringStream::create($protected));
$alg = $headers->get(1)->normalize(); // the algorithm label

Verifying the signature means rebuilding the Sig_structure of the specification and handing it to a signature algorithm, which is outside what this library does. web-auth/cose-lib does it, on top of this one: use it rather than assembling the pieces yourself.

docs.title: Sensor data
docs.text:
The case CBOR was designed for: a measurement, an instant, and as few bytes as possible on the wire.

use CBOR\MapObject;
use CBOR\Tag\DecimalFractionTag;
use CBOR\Tag\TimestampTag;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;

$sensorData = MapObject::create()
    ->add(
        TextStringObject::create('temperature'),
        DecimalFractionTag::createFromFloat(23.5)
    )
    ->add(
        TextStringObject::create('humidity'),
        UnsignedIntegerObject::create(65)
    )
    ->add(
        TextStringObject::create('timestamp'),
        TimestampTag::create(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(time()))
    );

$encoded = (string) $sensorData;

Two choices are worth noticing.

The temperature goes in as a decimal fraction rather than a float: 23.5 stays 23.5, where a binary float would carry a value that only prints as 23.5. It needs ext-bcmath at both ends.

The instant is tagged, so the reader gets a DateTimeImmutable without being told which of the numbers in the map was a date.

Shorter still: integer keys instead of text ones. 1, 2, 3 cost one byte each where "temperature" costs twelve, which is how CoAP and SenML payloads are written — at the price of needing the table of meanings on both sides.

$sensorData = MapObject::create()
    ->add(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(1), DecimalFractionTag::createFromFloat(23.5))
    ->add(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(2), UnsignedIntegerObject::create(65))
    ->add(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(3), TimestampTag::create(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(time())));

docs.title: WebAuthn and FIDO2
docs.text:
A WebAuthn registration hands the server an attestation object: CBOR, and the reason this library exists. It is a map of three entries — the attestation format, the statement itself, and the authenticator data as raw bytes:

use CBOR\Decoder;
use CBOR\MapObject;
use CBOR\StringStream;

$decoder = Decoder::create();

$attestationObject = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create($binaryData));

if (! $attestationObject instanceof MapObject) {
    throw new RuntimeException('An attestation object is a CBOR map');
}

$format = $attestationObject->get('fmt')->normalize();       // "packed", "none", "tpm"…
$statement = $attestationObject->get('attStmt');             // a map, whose shape depends on the format
$authenticatorData = $attestationObject->get('authData')->getValue(); // bytes, left as they are

Keep authData as the byte string it is. It is signed, so a single byte re-encoded differently breaks the signature; parse it as the binary structure WebAuthn specifies — flags, counter, credential — not as CBOR.

The credential public key, on the other hand, sits inside authData and is CBOR: a COSE key, a map whose keys are negative and positive integers rather than strings.

// $credentialPublicKey are the bytes that follow the credential id in authData
$key = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create($credentialPublicKey));

$kty = $key->get(1)->normalize();  // key type
$alg = $key->get(3)->normalize();  // algorithm

Do not write a WebAuthn server by hand

web-auth/webauthn-framework does all of the above, with the attestation statement formats, the verification of the signature and the checks the specification asks for. It uses this library underneath. The code here is for reading what is on the wire, or for debugging what a client sent.

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
A decoder reads a stream and returns the object tree it holds.

use CBOR\Decoder;
use CBOR\StringStream;

$binaryData = hex2bin('6548656c6c6f');
$stream = StringStream::create($binaryData);

$object = Decoder::create()->decode($stream);

if ($object instanceof TextStringObject) {
    echo $object->getValue();  // "Hello"
    echo $object->normalize(); // "Hello"
}

docs.title: Building a decoder
docs.text:
Decoder::create() with no argument knows every tag the library ships with and every simple value. A decoder can also be given exactly what it should recognise, and nothing else:

use CBOR\Decoder;
use CBOR\OtherObject\OtherObjectManager;
use CBOR\Tag\TagManager;

$tagManager = TagManager::create()
    ->add(TimestampTag::class)
    ->add(DatetimeTag::class);

$otherObjectManager = OtherObjectManager::create()
    ->add(TrueObject::class)
    ->add(FalseObject::class)
    ->add(NullObject::class);

$decoder = Decoder::create($tagManager, $otherObjectManager);

A tag number the manager does not know is not an error: it comes back as a GenericTag, which keeps the number and the value without interpreting them. Registering your own classes is described in registering a tag.

A decoder holds no state about the document it read, so build one once and reuse it.

docs.title: Limiting the nesting depth
docs.text:
Decoding is recursive: a deeply nested data item — thousands of nested arrays, maps or tags — can exhaust the call stack. The decoder therefore rejects data nested deeper than Decoder::DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH, 1000 levels, with an InvalidArgumentException.

When the data comes from an untrusted source, a much lower limit is wise:

// Accept at most 32 levels of nested arrays, maps and tags
$decoder = Decoder::create(null, null, 32);

docs.title: The cost of a hostile document
docs.text:
Normalizing a decoded object turns it into native PHP values, and a few tags expand far beyond the bytes they occupy. Two bounds keep that expansion proportionate to the input:

  • DecimalFractionTag::MAX_ABSOLUTE_EXPONENT and BigFloatTag::MAX_ABSOLUTE_EXPONENT, both 1024, cap the exponent of tags 4 and 5. Writing 10^e down takes about e digits, so an unbounded exponent turns a six-byte item into kilobytes.
  • UnsignedBigIntegerTag::MAX_BYTE_LENGTH and NegativeBigIntegerTag::MAX_BYTE_LENGTH, both 256 bytes — a 2048-bit integer — cap the byte string of tags 2 and 3.

A value outside either bound is rejected with an InvalidArgumentException.

A map key is normalized as the map is built, so both bounds apply during decode() itself, not only when you call normalize() later.

Install ext-gmp for untrusted input

Without it, brick/math converts the byte string of a big number to its decimal form in time quadratic in the length, which is several orders of magnitude slower than GMP. A document full of 256-byte bignums is cheap to write and expensive to read.

docs.title: Telling what you got
docs.text:
The tree a decoder returns says what the document actually contained, so instanceof is how you read it:

$object = $decoder->decode($stream);

// The major type
if ($object instanceof UnsignedIntegerObject) {
    echo 'Unsigned integer: ' . $object->getValue();
}

// A tag
if ($object instanceof TimestampTag) {
    echo 'Timestamp: ' . $object->normalize()->format('Y-m-d');
}

// Anything that gives a native value
if ($object instanceof Normalizable) {
    $phpValue = $object->normalize();
}

// All of it at once
$value = match (true) {
    $object instanceof TextStringObject => $object->getValue(),
    $object instanceof UnsignedIntegerObject => (int) $object->getValue(),
    $object instanceof ListObject => $object->normalize(),
    default => null,
};

Check the type before you trust the shape: a document from elsewhere holds what its sender chose, not what your application expects.

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text: There are two ways round. Encoder takes a native PHP value and hands back the bytes; building the objects yourself takes longer and lets you say exactly what goes on the wire.

docs.title: From PHP values
docs.text:
use CBOR\Encoder;

$encoder = new Encoder();

$encoder->encode(['name' => 'Alice', 'age' => 30]);
// a2 646e616d65 65416c696365 63616765 181e — a map of two entries

$encoder->encode([1, 2, 3]);   // 83 01 02 03 — an array
$encoder->encode('héllo');     // 66 … — a text string: the string is valid UTF-8
$encoder->encode("\x00\xff");  // 42 00ff — a byte string: this one is not
$encoder->encode(1.5);         // fb … — a double
$encoder->encode(null);        // f6

The mapping it applies:

PHP CBOR int unsigned or negative integer, by sign float double precision float string that is valid UTF-8 text string any other string byte string a list array array any other array map true, false, null the matching simple value a CBORObject itself, untouched

Anything else — an object, an enum, a resource — raises an InvalidArgumentException. The last row is what makes the two ways round meet: an object you built by hand can sit inside an array you hand to encode(), which is how a tagged value joins an otherwise plain structure.

use CBOR\Tag\TimestampTag;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;

$encoder->encode([
    'temperature' => 23,
    'at' => TimestampTag::create(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(time())),
]);

Five flags change how it writes, combined with | in the second argument:

$encoder->encode(1.5, Encoder::FLOAT_FORMAT_SINGLE_PRECISION);  // fa 3fc00000, four bytes instead of eight
$encoder->encode([1, 2], Encoder::INDEFINITE_LIST_LENGTH);      // 9f 01 02 ff
$encoder->encode(['a' => [1]], Encoder::INDEFINITE_MAP_LENGTH | Encoder::INDEFINITE_LIST_LENGTH);

FLOAT_FORMAT_SINGLE_PRECISION writes a float on four bytes rather than eight; INDEFINITE_TEXT_STRING_LENGTH, INDEFINITE_BYTE_STRING_LENGTH, INDEFINITE_LIST_LENGTH and INDEFINITE_MAP_LENGTH write the indefinite-length form of each kind. A flag applies to the whole document, not to one item of it.

In a Symfony application, the bundle wires this encoder into the Serializer, and these flags become options of the serialization context.

docs.title: Building the objects yourself
docs.text:
Every class provides a static create() method:

// Integers
$uint = UnsignedIntegerObject::create(42);
$nint = NegativeIntegerObject::create(-42);

// Strings
$text = TextStringObject::create('Hello World');
$bytes = ByteStringObject::create('binary data');

// Collections
$list = ListObject::create([
    UnsignedIntegerObject::create(1),
    UnsignedIntegerObject::create(2),
]);

$map = MapObject::create()
    ->add(TextStringObject::create('name'), TextStringObject::create('Alice'))
    ->add(TextStringObject::create('age'), UnsignedIntegerObject::create(30));

// Tags
$timestamp = TimestampTag::create(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(time()));

A list and a map are described in lists and maps; the tags, in tags.

docs.title: To bytes
docs.text:
Every object implements __toString(), so casting it encodes it:

$object = TextStringObject::create('Hello');
$encoded = (string) $object;
// or
$encoded = $object->__toString();

echo bin2hex($encoded); // "6548656c6c6f"

Encoding the outermost object encodes everything it holds. The result is a binary string: send it as application/cbor, store it, sign it.

docs.title: Choosing a type
docs.text:
Nothing guesses for you, which is the point: the type you pick is the type that goes on the wire. Two rules cover most cases.

  • Pick the narrowest integer class that holds the value. UnsignedIntegerObject writes the shortest head CBOR allows for the number you give it.
  • Pick a byte string for bytes and a text string for text. A TextStringObject is meant to hold valid UTF-8; binary data belongs in a ByteStringObject, where it costs nothing to carry.

When a value needs to say what it means — an instant rather than a number, a URI rather than a string — wrap it in a tag.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
The library uses the exceptions of PHP itself, with no hierarchy of its own to catch:

use InvalidArgumentException;
use RuntimeException;

try {
    $decoder = Decoder::create();
    $object = $decoder->decode($stream);
} catch (InvalidArgumentException $e) {
    // The document is not valid CBOR, or a value is outside the bounds the library enforces
    error_log('CBOR decoding error: ' . $e->getMessage());
} catch (RuntimeException $e) {
    // An extension the data asks for is missing
    error_log('Runtime error: ' . $e->getMessage());
}

InvalidArgumentException is what a malformed or hostile document raises:

  • a head that announces more bytes than the stream holds, or a break where none belongs;
  • nesting deeper than the limit the decoder was given;
  • a value outside the bounds that keep a document affordable;
  • a map with a duplicate key;
  • a tag whose content is not what the tag allows — a date-time string that is not a date, a decimal fraction that is not a pair of integers.

RuntimeException means the environment is short of something, not that the data is wrong: a decimal fraction or a bigfloat arrived and ext-bcmath is not installed, for instance.

Both are raised while building objects too, not only while decoding: DatetimeTag::create() with a text string that is not an RFC 3339 date-time fails at once, rather than on the far side of the wire.

Decode inside a try block, always

Every byte of an incoming document is attacker-controlled, including the ones that decide how much work the decoder does. Catch InvalidArgumentException around decode() and treat it as a rejected request, not as a bug.

docs.title: Indefinite-length objects
docs.text:
CBOR can encode a string, an array or a map without announcing its length: the item opens, its parts follow, and a break marks the end. It is what lets a producer start writing before it knows how much there is to write.

Four classes carry that form, and build up the same way as their definite-length counterparts:

// Indefinite-length text string
$text = IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject::create()
    ->append('Hello')
    ->append(' ')
    ->append('World');

echo $text->getValue(); // "Hello World"

// Indefinite-length byte string
$bytes = IndefiniteLengthByteStringObject::create()
    ->append('part1')
    ->append('part2');

// Indefinite-length list
$list = IndefiniteLengthListObject::create()
    ->add(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(1))
    ->add(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(2));

// Indefinite-length map
$map = IndefiniteLengthMapObject::create()
    ->add(TextStringObject::create('key1'), UnsignedIntegerObject::create(1))
    ->add(TextStringObject::create('key2'), UnsignedIntegerObject::create(2));

Indefinite-length lists and maps are Countable, just like their definite-length counterparts, so count() works whichever encoding a document uses:

$decoded = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create($data));
$count = count($decoded);

The same holds for normalization and iteration: code that reads a decoded document does not need to know which of the two forms it was written in. The decoder returns the class matching what it read, and both classes answer the same calls.

docs.title: Lists and maps
docs.text: An array (major type 4) is a ListObject, a map (major type 5) a MapObject. Both are Countable and IteratorAggregate, and both normalize to a PHP array.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
$list = ListObject::create();

// Add items
$list->add(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(1));
$list->add(TextStringObject::create('two'));

// Access items
$first = $list->get(0);
$count = $list->count();

// Check existence
if ($list->has(1)) {
    // …
}

// Remove items
$list->remove(0);

// Array access
$list[0] = UnsignedIntegerObject::create(42);
$value = $list[0];

// Iteration
foreach ($list as $item) {
    // …
}

// Normalize to a PHP array
$phpArray = $list->normalize();

docs.title: Maps
docs.text:
A map holds MapItem objects, each one a key and a value, both of them CBOR objects: a map key is not restricted to a string.

$map = MapObject::create();

// Add key-value pairs
$map->add(
    TextStringObject::create('name'),
    TextStringObject::create('Alice')
);

// A map may also be built from MapItem objects. Duplicate keys are rejected,
// as are two keys of different major types that resolve to the same offset.
$map = MapObject::create([
    MapItem::create(TextStringObject::create('name'), TextStringObject::create('Alice')),
    MapItem::create(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(1), UnsignedIntegerObject::create(2)),
]);

// Access values
$name = $map->get('name');

// Check existence
if ($map->has('name')) {
    // …
}

// Remove entries
$map->remove('name');

// Count entries
$count = $map->count();

// Iteration
foreach ($map as $item) {
    $key = $item->getKey();
    $value = $item->getValue();
}

// Normalize to a PHP array
$phpArray = $map->normalize();

get(), has() and remove() take the normalized key, not the key object: 'name' for a text string, 1 for an integer.

Order is kept

A map keeps its entries in the order they were added, and encodes them in that order. CBOR does not require a particular order; if a protocol asks for one — a canonical or deterministic encoding — it is for you to add the entries accordingly.

docs.title: Streams
docs.text:
A decoder does not read a string, it reads a Stream. The library ships with StringStream, which reads from a string already in memory:

use CBOR\StringStream;

$stream = StringStream::create($binaryData);
$object = $decoder->decode($stream);

A stream is consumed as the document is read, so one stream decodes one document. Several data items written one after another are read with several decode() calls on the same stream.

docs.title: Another source
docs.text:
Implement the Stream interface to decode from somewhere else — a file, a socket, a buffer filled as it arrives:

use CBOR\Stream;

class FileStream implements Stream
{
    private $handle;
    private int $position = 0;

    public function __construct(string $filepath)
    {
        $this->handle = fopen($filepath, 'rb');
    }

    public function read(int $length): string
    {
        $data = fread($this->handle, $length);
        $this->position += strlen($data);
        return $data;
    }

    public function getPosition(): int
    {
        return $this->position;
    }

    // … implement the remaining methods
}

// Use it with a decoder
$stream = new FileStream('/path/to/cbor/file.cbor');
$object = $decoder->decode($stream);

read() is asked for an exact number of bytes and is expected to return them. Returning fewer means the document ended in the middle of an item, which the decoder reports as an error: decide there whether to wait for more bytes or to fail.

docs.title: The built-in tags
docs.text: Each tag below has a class, a number, and rules about what it may wrap. A tag the library does not implement is still decoded: see the IANA registry.

docs.title: Tag 0 — a date-time string
docs.text:
A date and time written in the format of RFC 3339.

Class CBOR\Tag\DatetimeTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.1 Accepts TextStringObject or IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject Normalizes to DateTimeImmutable 
use CBOR\Tag\DatetimeTag;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;

$tag = DatetimeTag::create(
    TextStringObject::create('2024-01-15T10:30:00Z')
);

$dateTime = $tag->normalize();
echo $dateTime->format('Y-m-d H:i:s'); // 2024-01-15 10:30:00

A date-time that does not exist — 2013-02-30T12:00:00Z, a twenty-fifth hour — is rejected with an InvalidArgumentException rather than silently rolled over to the following day. A leap second is accepted and reported as the instant that follows it, since PHP dates cannot hold one.

docs.title: Tag 1 — an epoch timestamp
docs.text:
A POSIX timestamp: seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.

Class CBOR\Tag\TimestampTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.2 Accepts UnsignedIntegerObject, NegativeIntegerObject or a float object Normalizes to DateTimeImmutable 
use CBOR\Tag\TimestampTag;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;

$tag = TimestampTag::create(
    UnsignedIntegerObject::create(time())
);

$dateTime = $tag->normalize();
echo $dateTime->format('c');

A float timestamp is converted to the nearest microsecond. NAN, INF and magnitudes no date object can hold are rejected with an InvalidArgumentException.

docs.title: Big numbers
docs.text:
An empty byte string is the preferred serialization of zero (RFC 8949 § 3.4.3): tag 2 normalizes it to "0" and tag 3 to "-1".

Both tags are bounded

The byte string shall not exceed MAX_BYTE_LENGTH, 256 bytes — a 2048-bit integer; a longer one is rejected with an InvalidArgumentException. Turning it into the decimal string normalize() returns is a base conversion, which brick/math performs in time quadratic in the length on every calculator but GMP. Install ext-gmp when the input is untrusted.

docs.title: Tag 2 — an unsigned bignum
docs.text:
An arbitrarily large positive integer, as a byte string holding its big-endian representation.

Class CBOR\Tag\UnsignedBigIntegerTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.3 Accepts ByteStringObject or IndefiniteLengthByteStringObject Normalizes to a numeric string 
use CBOR\ByteStringObject;
use CBOR\Tag\UnsignedBigIntegerTag;

$tag = UnsignedBigIntegerTag::create(
    ByteStringObject::create(hex2bin('0123456789ABCDEF'))
);

$value = $tag->normalize(); // "81985529216486895"

docs.title: Tag 3 — a negative bignum
docs.text:
An arbitrarily large negative integer: the value is −1 minus the unsigned integer the byte string holds.

Class CBOR\Tag\NegativeBigIntegerTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.3 Accepts ByteStringObject or IndefiniteLengthByteStringObject Normalizes to a numeric string 
use CBOR\ByteStringObject;
use CBOR\Tag\NegativeBigIntegerTag;

// The value is -1 - unsigned_value
$tag = NegativeBigIntegerTag::create(
    ByteStringObject::create(hex2bin('FF'))
);

$value = $tag->normalize(); // "-256"

docs.title: Tag 4 — a decimal fraction
docs.text:
A number written as mantissa × 10^exponent.

Class CBOR\Tag\DecimalFractionTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.4 Requires ext-bcmath Accepts ListObject or IndefiniteLengthListObject of exactly two elements, [exponent, mantissa] Normalizes to the exact decimal value, as a string 
use CBOR\ListObject;
use CBOR\NegativeIntegerObject;
use CBOR\Tag\DecimalFractionTag;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;

// From an exponent and a mantissa: 1234 × 10^-2 = 12.34
$tag = DecimalFractionTag::createFromExponentAndMantissa(
    NegativeIntegerObject::create(-2),  // exponent
    UnsignedIntegerObject::create(1234) // mantissa
);

echo $tag->normalize(); // "12.34"

// From a PHP float
$tag = DecimalFractionTag::createFromFloat(3.14159, precision: 5);
echo $tag->normalize(); // "3.14159"

// From the list itself
$tag = DecimalFractionTag::create(
    ListObject::create([
        NegativeIntegerObject::create(-2),
        UnsignedIntegerObject::create(1234),
    ])
);

docs.title: Tag 5 — a bigfloat
docs.text:
A number written as mantissa × 2^exponent.

Class CBOR\Tag\BigFloatTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.4 Requires ext-bcmath Accepts ListObject of exactly two elements, [exponent, mantissa] Normalizes to the value as a string 
use CBOR\NegativeIntegerObject;
use CBOR\Tag\BigFloatTag;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;

// 5 × 2^-2 = 1.25
$tag = BigFloatTag::createFromExponentAndMantissa(
    NegativeIntegerObject::create(-2), // exponent, base 2
    UnsignedIntegerObject::create(5)   // mantissa
);

echo $tag->normalize(); // "1.25"

// From a PHP float
$tag = BigFloatTag::createFromFloat(3.14159);

The exponent is bounded

Its absolute value shall not exceed MAX_ABSOLUTE_EXPONENT, 1024; beyond it the tag is rejected with an InvalidArgumentException. Writing 10^e down takes about e digits, and 2^-e exactly e, so an unbounded exponent lets a six-byte item expand into kilobytes.

docs.title: Expected encodings
docs.text:
Tags 21, 22 and 23 say how the byte string they wrap is meant to be written out when the data is converted to a text format such as JSON. They are a hint and nothing more: the byte string is stored as it is, and the conversion is left to the application. None of the three implements Normalizable; each hands back the object it wraps through getValue().

All three accept a ByteStringObject or an IndefiniteLengthByteStringObject, and all three are specified in RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.2.

Tag Expected encoding Class 21 base64url CBOR\Tag\Base64UrlEncodingTag 22 base64 CBOR\Tag\Base64EncodingTag 23 base16, that is hexadecimal CBOR\Tag\Base16EncodingTag 
use CBOR\ByteStringObject;
use CBOR\Tag\Base64UrlEncodingTag;

$tag = Base64UrlEncodingTag::create(
    ByteStringObject::create('Hello World!')
);

$bytes = $tag->getValue()->normalize(); // "Hello World!"
$encoded = rtrim(strtr(base64_encode($bytes), '+/', '-_'), '='); // "SGVsbG8gV29ybGQh"

docs.title: Tag 32 — a URI
docs.text:
The text string holds a URI, as defined by RFC 3986.

Class CBOR\Tag\UriTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.3 Accepts TextStringObject or IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject Normalizes to the URI, as a string 
use CBOR\Tag\UriTag;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;

$tag = UriTag::create(
    TextStringObject::create('https://example.com/path?query=value')
);

$uri = $tag->normalize(); // "https://example.com/path?query=value"

docs.title: Tags 33 and 34 — text that is already encoded
docs.text:
The text string holds data that has already been encoded, base64url for tag 33 and base64 for tag 34. Where tags 21 and 22 announce an encoding still to be applied, these two describe text as it stands.

Both accept a TextStringObject or an IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject, and both are specified in RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.2.

Tag Content Class 33 base64url encoded text CBOR\Tag\Base64UrlTag 34 base64 encoded text CBOR\Tag\Base64Tag 
use CBOR\Tag\Base64UrlTag;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;

$tag = Base64UrlTag::create(
    TextStringObject::create('SGVsbG8gV29ybGQh')
);

docs.title: Tag 36 — a MIME message
docs.text:
The string holds a MIME message, an email among other things.

Class CBOR\Tag\MimeTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.3 Accepts TextStringObject, IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject, ByteStringObject or IndefiniteLengthByteStringObject 
use CBOR\Tag\MimeTag;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;

$mimeMessage = "Content-Type: text/plain\r\n\r\nHello World!";

$tag = MimeTag::create(
    TextStringObject::create($mimeMessage)
);

docs.title: Tag 24 — an encoded CBOR data item
docs.text:
The byte string holds a CBOR document of its own, not yet decoded. It is how a signed or encrypted payload travels: the bytes must stay exactly as they were to be verified.

Class CBOR\Tag\CBOREncodingTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.1 Accepts ByteStringObject 
use CBOR\ByteStringObject;
use CBOR\Tag\CBOREncodingTag;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;

// Encode a CBOR object
$innerObject = UnsignedIntegerObject::create(42);
$encoded = (string) $innerObject;

// Wrap it in tag 24
$tag = CBOREncodingTag::create(
    ByteStringObject::create($encoded)
);

// Decode it whenever you need it
$decoder = Decoder::create();
$decoded = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create($tag->getValue()->getValue()));

docs.title: Tag 55799 — self-described CBOR
docs.text:
A magic number that marks the start of a CBOR document, so that a reader can tell what it is holding without parsing it. Encoded, it is the three bytes d9 d9 f7.

Class CBOR\Tag\CBORTag Specification RFC 8949 § 3.4.6 Accepts any CBORObject Normalizes to whatever the wrapped object normalizes to 
use CBOR\MapObject;
use CBOR\Tag\CBORTag;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;

$data = MapObject::create()
    ->add(TextStringObject::create('key'), TextStringObject::create('value'));

$selfDescribed = CBORTag::create($data);

// Encoded, this starts with the bytes d9 d9 f7
$encoded = (string) $selfDescribed;

// The wrapped object
$innerObject = $selfDescribed->getValue();

// Or straight through to the wrapped value
$value = $selfDescribed->normalize();

SelfDescribeCBORTag is deprecated

CBOR\Tag\SelfDescribeCBORTag also declares tag 55799, and was documented here until 3.3.5. A tag manager registers one class per tag number, and CBORTag is the one the default decoder uses, so decoding a self-described document always yields a CBORTag. Use CBORTag; SelfDescribeCBORTag will be removed in 4.0.0. Its getCBORObject() is a duplicate of the inherited getValue().

docs.title: Three tags, written out
docs.text:
The three tags below follow the steps of the previous page through to working code: a tag that marks a text string, one that carries a structure, and one that enforces a set of rules on what it is given.

The numbers they use are illustrations. Look yours up in the IANA registry before you settle on it: a number already registered means a reader you did not write will misread your documents.

docs.title: An email tag
docs.text:
A tag that marks text strings as email addresses.

namespace App\CBOR\Tag;

use CBOR\CBORObject;
use CBOR\IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject;
use CBOR\Normalizable;
use CBOR\Tag;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;
use InvalidArgumentException;

/**
 * Tag 64000: Email Address (any number the IANA registry leaves unassigned)
 * Marks a text string as an RFC 5322 email address
 */
final class EmailTag extends Tag implements Normalizable
{
    private const TAG_EMAIL = 64000;

    public function __construct(
        int $additionalInformation,
        ?string $data,
        CBORObject $object
    ) {
        if (!$object instanceof TextStringObject
            && !$object instanceof IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException(
                'EmailTag only accepts text strings'
            );
        }

        // Validate email format
        $email = $object->getValue();
        if (!filter_var($email, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException(
                'Invalid email address format'
            );
        }

        parent::__construct($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }

    public static function getTagId(): int
    {
        return self::TAG_EMAIL;
    }

    public static function createFromLoadedData(
        int $additionalInformation,
        ?string $data,
        CBORObject $object
    ): Tag {
        return new self($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }

    public static function create(CBORObject $object): self
    {
        [$ai, $data] = self::determineComponents(self::TAG_EMAIL);
        return new self($ai, $data, $object);
    }

    public static function createFromEmail(string $email): self
    {
        return self::create(TextStringObject::create($email));
    }

    public function normalize(): string
    {
        /** @var TextStringObject|IndefiniteLengthTextStringObject $object */
        $object = $this->object;
        return $object->normalize();
    }

    public function getEmail(): string
    {
        return $this->normalize();
    }
}

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
use CBOR\Tag\EmailTag;

// Create
$email = EmailTag::createFromEmail('user@example.com');
$encoded = (string) $email;

// Decode
$decoder = Decoder::create();
$decoded = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create($encoded));

if ($decoded instanceof EmailTag) {
    echo $decoded->getEmail(); // user@example.com
}

docs.title: Geographic coordinates
docs.text:
A tag for WGS84 coordinates (latitude, longitude, altitude).

namespace App\CBOR\Tag;

use CBOR\CBORObject;
use CBOR\ListObject;
use CBOR\Normalizable;
use CBOR\Tag;
use CBOR\OtherObject\DoublePrecisionFloatObject;
use InvalidArgumentException;

/**
 * Tag 103: Geographic Coordinates (WGS-84)
 * Array of [latitude, longitude, altitude (optional)]
 */
final class GeoCoordinatesTag extends Tag implements Normalizable
{
    private const TAG_GEO_COORDINATES = 103;

    public function __construct(
        int $additionalInformation,
        ?string $data,
        CBORObject $object
    ) {
        if (!$object instanceof ListObject) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException(
                'GeoCoordinatesTag requires a ListObject'
            );
        }

        $count = count($object);
        if ($count < 2 || $count > 3) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException(
                'GeoCoordinates must have 2 or 3 elements [lat, lon, alt?]'
            );
        }

        // Validate latitude
        $lat = $object->get(0);
        if (!$this->isNumeric($lat)) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('Latitude must be numeric');
        }

        // Validate longitude
        $lon = $object->get(1);
        if (!$this->isNumeric($lon)) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('Longitude must be numeric');
        }

        // Validate altitude if present
        if ($count === 3) {
            $alt = $object->get(2);
            if (!$this->isNumeric($alt)) {
                throw new InvalidArgumentException('Altitude must be numeric');
            }
        }

        parent::__construct($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }

    private function isNumeric(CBORObject $object): bool
    {
        return $object instanceof UnsignedIntegerObject
            || $object instanceof NegativeIntegerObject
            || $object instanceof DoublePrecisionFloatObject
            || $object instanceof SinglePrecisionFloatObject;
    }

    public static function getTagId(): int
    {
        return self::TAG_GEO_COORDINATES;
    }

    public static function createFromLoadedData(
        int $additionalInformation,
        ?string $data,
        CBORObject $object
    ): Tag {
        return new self($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }

    public static function create(CBORObject $object): self
    {
        [$ai, $data] = self::determineComponents(self::TAG_GEO_COORDINATES);
        return new self($ai, $data, $object);
    }

    public static function createFromCoordinates(
        float $latitude,
        float $longitude,
        ?float $altitude = null
    ): self {
        $list = ListObject::create([
            DoublePrecisionFloatObject::createFromFloat($latitude),
            DoublePrecisionFloatObject::createFromFloat($longitude),
        ]);

        if ($altitude !== null) {
            $list->add(DoublePrecisionFloatObject::createFromFloat($altitude));
        }

        return self::create($list);
    }

    /**
     * @return array{latitude: float, longitude: float, altitude: float|null}
     */
    public function normalize(): array
    {
        /** @var ListObject $list */
        $list = $this->object;

        $result = [
            'latitude' => (float) $list->get(0)->normalize(),
            'longitude' => (float) $list->get(1)->normalize(),
            'altitude' => null,
        ];

        if (count($list) === 3) {
            $result['altitude'] = (float) $list->get(2)->normalize();
        }

        return $result;
    }

    public function getLatitude(): float
    {
        /** @var ListObject $list */
        $list = $this->object;
        return (float) $list->get(0)->normalize();
    }

    public function getLongitude(): float
    {
        /** @var ListObject $list */
        $list = $this->object;
        return (float) $list->get(1)->normalize();
    }

    public function getAltitude(): ?float
    {
        /** @var ListObject $list */
        $list = $this->object;

        if (count($list) === 3) {
            return (float) $list->get(2)->normalize();
        }

        return null;
    }
}

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
use CBOR\Tag\GeoCoordinatesTag;

// Create coordinates for Paris, France
$coords = GeoCoordinatesTag::createFromCoordinates(
    48.8566,  // latitude
    2.3522,   // longitude
    35.0      // altitude (meters)
);

$normalized = $coords->normalize();
/*
[
    'latitude' => 48.8566,
    'longitude' => 2.3522,
    'altitude' => 35.0
]
*/

echo $coords->getLatitude();  // 48.8566
echo $coords->getLongitude(); // 2.3522
echo $coords->getAltitude();  // 35.0

docs.title: A tag that validates
docs.text:
A tag with multiple validation rules and transformation logic.

namespace App\CBOR\Tag;

use CBOR\CBORObject;
use CBOR\MapObject;
use CBOR\Normalizable;
use CBOR\Tag;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;
use InvalidArgumentException;

/**
 * Tag 1000: User Profile
 * Structured user profile with validation
 */
final class UserProfileTag extends Tag implements Normalizable
{
    private const TAG_USER_PROFILE = 1000;

    private const REQUIRED_KEYS = ['username', 'email', 'age'];

    public function __construct(
        int $additionalInformation,
        ?string $data,
        CBORObject $object
    ) {
        if (!$object instanceof MapObject) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException(
                'UserProfileTag requires a MapObject'
            );
        }

        // Validate required keys
        foreach (self::REQUIRED_KEYS as $key) {
            if (!$object->has($key)) {
                throw new InvalidArgumentException(
                    "Missing required key: {$key}"
                );
            }
        }

        // Validate username
        $username = $object->get('username');
        if (!$username instanceof TextStringObject) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('Username must be a text string');
        }
        if (strlen($username->getValue()) < 3) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('Username must be at least 3 characters');
        }

        // Validate email
        $email = $object->get('email');
        if (!$email instanceof TextStringObject) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('Email must be a text string');
        }
        if (!filter_var($email->getValue(), FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('Invalid email format');
        }

        // Validate age
        $age = $object->get('age');
        if (!$age instanceof UnsignedIntegerObject) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('Age must be an unsigned integer');
        }
        $ageValue = (int) $age->getValue();
        if ($ageValue < 0 || $ageValue > 150) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('Age must be between 0 and 150');
        }

        parent::__construct($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }

    public static function getTagId(): int
    {
        return self::TAG_USER_PROFILE;
    }

    public static function createFromLoadedData(
        int $additionalInformation,
        ?string $data,
        CBORObject $object
    ): Tag {
        return new self($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }

    public static function create(CBORObject $object): self
    {
        [$ai, $data] = self::determineComponents(self::TAG_USER_PROFILE);
        return new self($ai, $data, $object);
    }

    public static function createFromArray(array $profile): self
    {
        $map = MapObject::create()
            ->add(
                TextStringObject::create('username'),
                TextStringObject::create($profile['username'])
            )
            ->add(
                TextStringObject::create('email'),
                TextStringObject::create($profile['email'])
            )
            ->add(
                TextStringObject::create('age'),
                UnsignedIntegerObject::create($profile['age'])
            );

        return self::create($map);
    }

    public function normalize(): array
    {
        /** @var MapObject $map */
        $map = $this->object;

        return [
            'username' => $map->get('username')->normalize(),
            'email' => $map->get('email')->normalize(),
            'age' => (int) $map->get('age')->normalize(),
        ];
    }
}

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
use CBOR\Tag\UserProfileTag;

// Create from array
$profile = UserProfileTag::createFromArray([
    'username' => 'john_doe',
    'email' => 'john@example.com',
    'age' => 30,
]);

// Validation happens automatically
try {
    $invalid = UserProfileTag::createFromArray([
        'username' => 'jo', // Too short!
        'email' => 'invalid-email',
        'age' => 30,
    ]);
} catch (InvalidArgumentException $e) {
    echo $e->getMessage(); // "Username must be at least 3 characters"
}

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
A tag is major type 6: an integer that prefixes a data item and says what that item means. The integer alone carries the meaning, and which integer means what is held in a registry maintained by IANA.

Tag(tag_number, data_item)

tag_number identifies the semantics; data_item is any CBOR object the tag applies to. Tag 1 in front of an integer, for instance, says that the integer is not a count but an instant — seconds since the epoch — which is why normalize() on it hands back a DateTimeImmutable rather than a number.

The library implements the tags applications meet most often, listed one by one in the built-in tags, and decodes the rest without interpreting them. Tags of your own are written the same way the built-in ones are: see writing a tag of your own.

docs.title: Encoding with a tag
docs.text:
A tag wraps an object:

use CBOR\Tag\TimestampTag;
use CBOR\UnsignedIntegerObject;

// The data
$timestamp = UnsignedIntegerObject::create(time());

// Wrapped in a tag
$tagged = TimestampTag::create($timestamp);

// Encoded
$encoded = (string) $tagged;

docs.title: Decoding a tag
docs.text:
A decoder recognises every tag it has been given a class for, and returns an object of that class:

use CBOR\Decoder;
use CBOR\StringStream;

$decoder = Decoder::create();
$decoded = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create($encoded));

if ($decoded instanceof TimestampTag) {
    $dateTime = $decoded->normalize();
    echo $dateTime->format('Y-m-d H:i:s');
}

docs.title: Reading a tagged value
docs.text:
// The wrapped object
$wrappedObject = $tagged->getValue();

// The additional data, if any
$data = $tagged->getData();

// The tag number
$tagId = $tagged::getTagId();

Most tags also implement Normalizable, which goes straight to the native value and skips the wrapped object: normalize() on a tag 0 returns a DateTimeImmutable, on a tag 2 the digits of the big integer. The ones that do not implement it are the tags whose content needs no conversion — see expected encodings.

docs.title: Working with tags well
docs.text:
• Prefer a registered tag. A number from the IANA registry is understood by readers you did not write; a private number is understood by yours alone.
  • Check the type you were handed. A tag constrains what it may wrap, but a document from elsewhere may use a tag number for something else entirely. Verify before you use it.
  • Expect tags you do not know. A number nothing is registered for decodes to a GenericTag; decide what your application does with one.
  • Mind the extensions. The decimal fraction and bigfloat tags need ext-bcmath, and the big number tags want ext-gmp. See installation.
  • Normalize at the edge. Turn tags into PHP values where the data enters your application, and work with the values afterwards.

docs.title: Registering and testing a tag
docs.text: A tag class encodes on its own, but a decoder only returns it if it has been told the class exists.

docs.title: Telling the decoder about it
docs.text:
use CBOR\Decoder;
use CBOR\Tag\TagManager;

$tagManager = TagManager::create()
    ->add(EmailTag::class)
    ->add(GeoCoordinatesTag::class)
    ->add(UserProfileTag::class);

$decoder = Decoder::create($tagManager);

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
// Encoding
$email = EmailTag::createFromEmail('user@example.com');
$encoded = (string) $email;

// Decoding
$decoded = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create($encoded));

if ($decoded instanceof EmailTag) {
    echo $decoded->getEmail();
}

A manager you build replaces the default set

Decoder::create() with no argument knows the fifteen built-in tags. Hand it a TagManager and that manager is the whole set: a tag 0 then decodes to a GenericTag, because nothing registered DatetimeTag any more. There is no public factory for "the defaults plus mine", so list them:

use CBOR\Tag\Base16EncodingTag;
use CBOR\Tag\Base64EncodingTag;
use CBOR\Tag\Base64Tag;
use CBOR\Tag\Base64UrlEncodingTag;
use CBOR\Tag\Base64UrlTag;
use CBOR\Tag\BigFloatTag;
use CBOR\Tag\CBOREncodingTag;
use CBOR\Tag\CBORTag;
use CBOR\Tag\DatetimeTag;
use CBOR\Tag\DecimalFractionTag;
use CBOR\Tag\MimeTag;
use CBOR\Tag\NegativeBigIntegerTag;
use CBOR\Tag\TimestampTag;
use CBOR\Tag\UnsignedBigIntegerTag;
use CBOR\Tag\UriTag;

$tagManager = TagManager::create([
    DatetimeTag::class, TimestampTag::class,
    UnsignedBigIntegerTag::class, NegativeBigIntegerTag::class,
    DecimalFractionTag::class, BigFloatTag::class,
    Base64UrlEncodingTag::class, Base64EncodingTag::class, Base16EncodingTag::class,
    CBOREncodingTag::class,
    UriTag::class, Base64UrlTag::class, Base64Tag::class, MimeTag::class,
    CBORTag::class,
])
    ->add(EmailTag::class)
    ->add(GeoCoordinatesTag::class);

Registering only your own tags is a sound choice too, when you know exactly what the documents you read may contain: anything else comes back as a GenericTag instead of being interpreted.

add() refuses a class whose getTagId() is negative, and a second class for a number already registered replaces the first: one class per number.

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text:
use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;

class EmailTagTest extends TestCase
{
    public function testCreateFromValidEmail(): void
    {
        $tag = EmailTag::createFromEmail('test@example.com');

        $this->assertInstanceOf(EmailTag::class, $tag);
        $this->assertSame('test@example.com', $tag->getEmail());
    }

    public function testRejectsInvalidEmail(): void
    {
        $this->expectException(InvalidArgumentException::class);
        EmailTag::createFromEmail('not-an-email');
    }

    public function testEncodingAndDecoding(): void
    {
        $original = EmailTag::createFromEmail('test@example.com');
        $encoded = (string) $original;

        $tagManager = TagManager::create()->add(EmailTag::class);
        $decoder = Decoder::create($tagManager);

        $decoded = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create($encoded));

        $this->assertInstanceOf(EmailTag::class, $decoded);
        $this->assertSame('test@example.com', $decoded->getEmail());
    }
}

docs.title: Tags from other specifications
docs.text: Several specifications define their own tag numbers, registered with IANA like any other. None of them has a class in this version of the library: implement the ones you need the way the pages above describe.

docs.title: COSE and CWT
docs.text:
COSE, RFC 9052, gives one tag per message type, and CWT, RFC 8392, one for a token:

Tag Structure 16 COSE_Encrypt0, encrypted, single recipient implied 17 COSE_Mac0, MACed, no recipient structure 18 COSE_Sign1, signed by one signer 61 CWT_Tag, a CBOR Web Token 96 COSE_Encrypt, encrypted, with recipients 97 COSE_Mac, MACed, with recipients 98 COSE_Sign, signed, with one or more signatures

A COSE_Sign1 is an array of four items — protected header, unprotected header, payload, signature — so the tag class has something precise to check:

namespace App\CBOR\Tag;

use CBOR\CBORObject;
use CBOR\ListObject;
use CBOR\Tag;
use InvalidArgumentException;

/**
 * Tag 18: COSE_Sign1, a message signed by a single signer.
 *
 * @see https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9052#section-4.2
 */
final class CoseSign1Tag extends Tag
{
    private const TAG_COSE_SIGN1 = 18;

    public function __construct(int $additionalInformation, ?string $data, CBORObject $object)
    {
        if (! $object instanceof ListObject || count($object) !== 4) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('COSE_Sign1 must be an array of 4 elements');
        }

        // [protected, unprotected, payload, signature]
        parent::__construct($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }

    public static function getTagId(): int
    {
        return self::TAG_COSE_SIGN1;
    }

    public static function createFromLoadedData(int $additionalInformation, ?string $data, CBORObject $object): Tag
    {
        return new self($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }
}

The protected header is itself a byte string holding a CBOR map, which is what lets a signature cover the exact bytes that were signed. Do not decode and re-encode it: keep the byte string as it arrived, as tag 24 does.

A CWT wraps one of those COSE structures, so its own class checks what it was handed:

public function __construct(int $additionalInformation, ?string $data, CBORObject $object)
{
    if (! $object instanceof CoseSign1Tag && ! $object instanceof CoseMac0Tag) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException('A CWT must wrap a COSE structure');
    }

    parent::__construct($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
}

For COSE itself — the headers, the algorithms, the keys, the signature verification — use web-auth/cose-lib, which is built on this library.

docs.title: Other specifications
docs.text:
• CoAP, RFC 7252, carries CBOR payloads, whose content formats may call for tags of their own.
  • SenML, RFC 8428, describes sensor measurements in CBOR, with its own labels and semantics.

Before you pick a number for something of your own, look it up in the IANA registry: a number already registered means someone else's reader will misunderstand your documents.

docs.title: The IANA registry
docs.text:
Tag numbers are held in the CBOR tags registry of IANA. The library implements the ones below; every other number still decodes, as a tag that keeps its number without interpreting it.

Tag Meaning Class Specification 0 Date-time string, RFC 3339 DatetimeTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.1 1 Epoch timestamp TimestampTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.2 2 Unsigned bignum UnsignedBigIntegerTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.3 3 Negative bignum NegativeBigIntegerTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.3 4 Decimal fraction DecimalFractionTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.4 5 Bigfloat BigFloatTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.4 21 base64url expected Base64UrlEncodingTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.2 22 base64 expected Base64EncodingTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.2 23 base16 expected Base16EncodingTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.2 24 Encoded CBOR data item CBOREncodingTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.1 32 URI UriTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.3 33 base64url encoded text Base64UrlTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.2 34 base64 encoded text Base64Tag RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.2 36 MIME message MimeTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.5.3 55799 Self-described CBOR CBORTag RFC 8949 § 3.4.6

Every class is in the CBOR\Tag namespace, and each one is described in the built-in tags.

docs.title: A tag the library does not know
docs.text:
A tag number no class is registered for is not an error: the decoder returns a GenericTag, which keeps the head and the object the tag wrapped, so a document survives a round trip through code that does not understand all of it. Its normalize() normalizes the wrapped item on its own, since the number carries no meaning the library knows.

GenericTag::getTagId() returns -1, because the class stands for no number in particular. The number itself is in the head of the item: it is the additional information when that is 23 or less, and the big-endian payload getData() returns otherwise.

use CBOR\CBORObject;
use CBOR\Tag\GenericTag;

function tagNumberOf(GenericTag $tag): int
{
    $ai = $tag->getAdditionalInformation();
    if ($ai <= 23) {
        return $ai;
    }

    $data = (string) $tag->getData();

    return match ($ai) {
        CBORObject::LENGTH_1_BYTE => ord($data),
        CBORObject::LENGTH_2_BYTES => unpack('n', $data)[1],
        CBORObject::LENGTH_4_BYTES => unpack('N', $data)[1],
        CBORObject::LENGTH_8_BYTES => unpack('J', $data)[1],
    };
}

$decoded = $decoder->decode(StringStream::create(hex2bin('d904d201')));

$decoded instanceof GenericTag;   // true
tagNumberOf($decoded);            // 1234
$decoded->getValue();             // UnsignedIntegerObject, the tagged item

When a number matters to your application, give it a class of its own — writing a tag of your own — and register that class with the decoder. The decoder then hands you that class instead of a GenericTag, and getTagId() answers properly.

docs.title: Writing a tag of your own
docs.text: Every tag in this library, the built-in ones included, is a class extending CBOR\Tag. Writing one is the same work: pick a number, extend the class, say what the tag accepts, and say what it normalizes to. This page is the recipe; three tags, written out follows it through to working code.

docs.title: When to write one
docs.text:
Write a tag of your own when you need to:

  • implement a tag another specification defines — COSE, CWT, a content format of CoAP;
  • give your own data a meaning the major types do not carry;
  • encode a structure that has rules about its shape, and have them checked on the way in;
  • interoperate with a system that already uses a registered tag;
  • make a document shorter, by letting the tag say what a key or a wrapper would otherwise have to.

docs.title: The shape of a tag class
docs.text:
Every tag of this library extends the abstract CBOR\Tag class. The shape is always this one:

namespace App\CBOR\Tag;

use CBOR\CBORObject;
use CBOR\Tag;

class MyCustomTag extends Tag
{
    // Required: Return the IANA tag number
    public static function getTagId(): int
    {
        return 1234; // Your tag number
    }

    // Required: Create tag from decoded data
    public static function createFromLoadedData(
        int $additionalInformation,
        ?string $data,
        CBORObject $object
    ): Tag {
        return new self($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }

    // Optional: Convenience constructor
    public static function create(CBORObject $object): self
    {
        [$ai, $data] = self::determineComponents(self::getTagId());
        return new self($ai, $data, $object);
    }
}

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• getTagId() returns the tag number the class stands for.
  • createFromLoadedData() is the factory the decoder calls.

docs.title: Optional
docs.text:
• create(), the convenience method that wraps an object in the tag.
  • normalize(), which turns the tag into a native PHP value; declare Normalizable with it.
  • Validation in the constructor, which is where a tag says what it accepts.

docs.title: 1. Choose a number
docs.text:
A tag number is not yours to invent freely: a tag means something because a reader elsewhere knows the number. CBOR has no private-use range — look yours up in the IANA registry before you settle on it.

  • Documents that stay inside your own systems can use any number nothing has registered. Take a high one, and write down what it means where the rest of your protocol is written down.
  • Documents that travel further need a number of their own. The registry gives out the numbers from 256 up on a first-come, first-served basis; below that, a registration needs a specification.
private const TAG_MY_CUSTOM = 64000;

docs.title: 2. Extend Tag
docs.text:
namespace App\CBOR\Tag;

use CBOR\CBORObject;
use CBOR\Tag;

final class MyCustomTag extends Tag
{
    private const TAG_NUMBER = 1234;

    public static function getTagId(): int
    {
        return self::TAG_NUMBER;
    }

    public static function createFromLoadedData(
        int $additionalInformation,
        ?string $data,
        CBORObject $object
    ): Tag {
        return new self($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
    }
}

docs.title: 3. Validate what it wraps
docs.text:
Validate the wrapped object in the constructor:

use InvalidArgumentException;
use CBOR\TextStringObject;

public function __construct(
    int $additionalInformation,
    ?string $data,
    CBORObject $object
) {
    // Validate that the object is the expected type
    if (!$object instanceof TextStringObject) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException(
            'MyCustomTag only accepts TextStringObject'
        );
    }

    // Add custom validation
    $value = $object->getValue();
    if (strlen($value) < 5) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException(
            'Value must be at least 5 characters'
        );
    }

    parent::__construct($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
}

docs.title: 4. Normalize to a PHP value
docs.text:
Implement the Normalizable interface to convert to PHP types:

use CBOR\Normalizable;

final class MyCustomTag extends Tag implements Normalizable
{
    public function normalize(): mixed
    {
        /** @var TextStringObject $object */
        $object = $this->object;

        // Custom transformation logic
        return strtoupper($object->getValue());
    }
}

docs.title: 5. Add the convenience you want
docs.text:
public static function create(CBORObject $object): self
{
    [$ai, $data] = self::determineComponents(self::TAG_NUMBER);
    return new self($ai, $data, $object);
}

public static function createFromString(string $value): self
{
    return self::create(TextStringObject::create($value));
}

docs.title: Nested tags
docs.text:
Tags can wrap other tagged values:

// Timestamp wrapped in a custom "audit log" tag
$timestamp = TimestampTag::create(UnsignedIntegerObject::create(time()));
$auditLog = AuditLogTag::create($timestamp);

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• Lazy Validation: Validate only when necessary
  • Caching: Cache normalized values if normalization is expensive
  • Type Checking: Use instanceof checks sparingly

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
public function __construct(
    int $additionalInformation,
    ?string $data,
    CBORObject $object
) {
    try {
        // Validation logic
        $this->validate($object);
    } catch (\Exception $e) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException(
            sprintf('Invalid %s: %s', static::class, $e->getMessage()),
            0,
            $e
        );
    }

    parent::__construct($additionalInformation, $data, $object);
}

docs.title: Writing a tag well
docs.text:
1. Use Appropriate Tag Numbers: Check IANA registry to avoid conflicts
  2. Validate Early: Validate in the constructor to fail fast
  3. Document Thoroughly: Include RFC references and usage examples
  4. Implement Normalizable: Make tags easy to work with
  5. Type-Safe: Use strict types and type hints
  6. Test Extensively: Test validation, encoding, and decoding
  7. Handle Edge Cases: Consider null values, empty collections, etc.
  8. Follow Specifications: When implementing standard tags, follow specs exactly
